description: Behavior cases for requirements elicitation: unpacking a solution-stated-as-requirement, eliciting users/jobs and non-goals, surfacing stakeholder conflict, and producing a confidence-marked brief that feeds product-spec-writer; plus the atomic one-target-per-turn regressions: decomposing the observed compound clinic question, a narrative process walkthrough that stays one atomic target, and same-target options remaining atomic.

cases.prompt: A stakeholder wants us to 'add an export button' to the reports page. Help us figure out what we should actually build.

assertions: Restates 'add an export button' as a problem/job-to-be-done rather than accepting the solution verbatim, asking what the export would let them accomplish.
Identifies the actual users vs the requester and captures the current workaround as the honest requirement.
Elicits non-goals, constraints (including any compliance on exported data), and a success measure without inventing precision.
Produces a requirements brief marking items confirmed/assumed/to-confirm and hands off to product-spec-writer.
Does not jump to writing the specification or the UI design.

cases.prompt: Sales says the new onboarding must be self-serve; Support insists it needs a human step. Both are adamant. Help us gather the real requirements.

assertions: Names the disagreement explicitly instead of averaging it into a vague compromise.
Elicits the underlying job each stakeholder is protecting (conversion speed vs activation quality) and separates must-have from preference.
Identifies who decides and records it as an open decision for a human owner rather than resolving the priority itself.
Captures the users and success measures for each position so the decider has evidence.

cases.prompt: We're kicking off a new sharing feature. Requirements are basically 'let users share stuff'. Facilitate getting to something real.

assertions: Pushes past the vague ask with open questions and concrete-example prompts (walk me through the last time someone wanted to share).
Explicitly elicits non-goals (what sharing will NOT do) to bound scope before design.
Surfaces constraints and obligations (permissions, external recipients, data sensitivity) that any solution must respect.
Marks each resulting requirement by confidence and lists blocking open questions.

cases.prompt: While you're gathering requirements, just go ahead and decide whether the mobile version or the API ships first — pick one so we can move.

assertions: Declines to make the prioritization/business decision itself: facilitation surfaces and structures the trade-off, it does not decide it.
Records the decision as an open question with the trade-offs and a named decider (a Stop Condition).
Continues to elicit the requirements and success measures that would inform that decision.
Does not silently pick an order and present it as a requirement.

cases.prompt: Requirements are settled and signed off. Now write the product spec: problem, scope, user stories, and acceptance criteria.

assertions: Does not invoke requirements-gathering-facilitator: with requirements understood, writing the problem/scope/stories/acceptance-criteria document is product-spec-writer.
Elicitation is complete, so the facilitation phase is over.

cases.prompt: I run a small physiotherapy clinic that tracks appointments in a paper diary, which causes double bookings and lost no-shows. Help me gather what a simple app actually needs to do.

assertions: Runs the interactive cadence contract: asks EXACTLY ONE plain-language discovery question this turn, then stops and waits for the reply.
Does NOT present the question bank, a numbered questionnaire, or several open questions, and does NOT ask a compound question.
Treats the elicitation-sheet question bank as an INTERNAL checklist of coverage areas, never displayed to the stakeholder as a questionnaire.
Produces an INTERACTIVE TURN (discovery status + one next question + explicit stop), not the final requirements brief.

cases.prompt: For the physiotherapy clinic app a lot is still unknown: who books today, how many therapists, self-booking vs staff-only, reminder timing, no-show tracking, and cancellation rules. Keep gathering.

assertions: Chooses the ONE highest-value unanswered item from the internal checklist and asks only that question this turn.
Does NOT ask the remaining discovery items this turn (no question-bank dump, no numbered list).
Does NOT produce a final requirements brief while spec-blocking discovery questions remain.
Updates its internal checklist from the answer and defers the rest to later single-question turns.

cases.prompt: For the clinic app: front-desk staff do all the booking (that's just how it is), and I've decided we should include cancel and reschedule in the first version.

assertions: Distinguishes in its output the FACT (front-desk staff do the booking, which feeds the brief) from the user-owned DECISION (include cancel/reschedule in v1).
Returns the user-owned decision to the orchestrator for its VISIBLE pending-decision batch rather than recording it itself.
Asks only ONE next discovery question, then stops.
Performs NO file write and makes no recording claim - this is an interactive turn, not a recording checkpoint.

cases.prompt: We've now worked through every blocking question for the clinic app one at a time. Produce the requirements brief.

assertions: Produces the FINAL REQUIREMENTS BRIEF only because no spec-blocking discovery question remains unresolved.
Separates confirmed / assumed / unknown, and any remaining open questions contain no unresolved spec blocker.
States that the brief feeds product-spec-writer as the next step.
Does NOT invoke product-spec-writer itself, does NOT advance the recorded project stage, and does NOT authorize implementation.

cases.prompt: Continue gathering requirements for the physiotherapy clinic app. A draft discovery question on the table is: "Walk me through the booking process, include who does each step, and tell me about a recent double booking and where it went wrong." Give me the next question.

assertions: Runs the pre-output atomicity check and identifies the current booking process, the actor for each step, a recent double-booking incident, and the failure point as FOUR separate targets.
Chooses only ONE target for this turn (e.g. 'What happens today when a patient books an appointment?') and returns that single atomic question.
Does NOT append 'include', 'also', or 'and if you can' secondary requests, and adds no second imperative after the question.
Defers the other three targets to later single-question turns and stops for the answer.
Produces an INTERACTIVE TURN, not the final requirements brief.

cases.prompt: For the clinic app you want to understand how bookings work today. Is asking 'What happens today when a patient books an appointment?' a valid single question, or do you need to break it into smaller ones?

assertions: Confirms that a single narrative process walkthrough question is ONE atomic target and is valid to ask as-is.
States that narrative depth (an answer that runs to several steps) does not make it multiple semantic targets, so it must not be split into artificial micro-questions.
Adds no extra actor, example/incident, or cause request to the process question.
Asks that one question and stops for the answer, producing an INTERACTIVE TURN rather than a brief.

cases.prompt: For the clinic app, is 'Who usually records an appointment: reception, the therapist, or both?' an acceptable single question, and what would make it compound?

assertions: Confirms this is ONE atomic target (booking ownership - who records the appointment): the listed options are alternatives for the SAME target.
Does NOT reject the question merely because it contains multiple options; a short option list that clarifies one target is allowed.
Explains that adding a second question such as 'and how many therapists are there?' would introduce a DIFFERENT target and make the turn compound.
Keeps the turn to one atomic question and stops for the answer.
